houses.name: House NE Quarter Row 1 (Maison nord-est quartier, 1ère rangée)
houses.notes: First row of northeast quarter has one insula east of small northern baths. Three shops open onto boulevard with back rooms. Central atrium now disappeared. East side has five variable-sized rooms with large vestibule extending onto street.

houses.name: House NE Quarter Row 2 Position 1 (Maison nord-est quartier, 2e rangée, position 1)
houses.notes: First square of second row on eastern side of Cardo, south of small baths. Door with three steps opens to vestibule with geometric mosaic pavement. Atrium with preserved column bases and well in center. Private baths to northeast with laconicum and furnace.; Cold plunge later converted into a baptistery for a Christian basilica the Byzantines installed over the east part of the house [ballu_1911_III printed p. 80]; Corner stone pierced obliquely for tethering horses; a second caldarium encroached on the street like the first [ballu_1911_III printed p. 80]; Besides the rooms named, seven further rooms plus a vestibule with entrance door on the east side [ballu_1911_III printed p. 80]

houses.name: House NE Quarter Row 2 Position 2 (Maison nord-est quartier, 2e rangée, position 2)
houses.notes: Second square east of previous, with four small shops on northern street. Remains of storage amphorae. Concrete basin in southwest corner. Interior wall traces poorly defined.; Anchor for mapping: the first carré of this row lies on the E flank of the Cardo nord, S of the petits thermes nord; this house is immediately east of it [ballu_1911_III printed p. 79]

houses.name: House NE Quarter Row 3 (Maison nord-est quartier, 3e rangée)
houses.notes: Third row of northeast quarter has one ruined insula south of previous house. Central atrium accessed via wide paved vestibule with two eastern street doors. Contains Byzantine stone table and nine mangers for horses.

houses.name: House NE Quarter Row 4 (Maison nord-est quartier, 4e rangée)
houses.notes: Fourth row of northeast quarter has three insulae. First insula on eastern Cardo with entrance on parallel road to Decumanus. Contains paved atrium with fountain on east side, six rooms in southern part, ten in northern part. Well-crafted water discharge stone.; Second block (2nd file N-S): brick water conduit 0.70 x 0.35 crossing a 10 x 8 m room; sandstone-paved atrium; mosaics in white/red/black squares-in-lozenges; a once-luxurious house later demolished and long occupied in 'barbarian' times; point-engraved dancer on a limestone slab [ballu_1911_III printed p. 81]; Third block east of the previous: paved atrium with basin on north face; ~13 rooms; judged of no great interest [ballu_1911_III printed p. 82]

houses.name: House of Optat (Maison d'Optat)
houses.notes: Complete peristyle. Many later modifications and alterations (remaniements).; Mosaic 191 carries a Christian inscription: 'I completed these works on the order of the bishop of God Optatus' — the eponym of the house [germain_1969_b printed p. 127]; NW corner of mosaic 190 was damaged by a potter's kiln installed later — evidence of post-residential productive reuse [germain_1969_b printed p. 126]; West portico of the court measures 14.20 x 2.80 m (mosaic 190 location) [germain_1969_b printed p. 124]

BUT Laghmouche Table 1 is on p.224 (not 254-255) and lists the NORTH house, not this one. — germain_1969_b printed p. 130, audit 2026-07-05]
houses.notes: Christofle 1938 (pp. 355-356, section '1° FOUILLES DE LA COLLINE AU SUD DU CAPITOLE') reports 1933 excavations on the hill south of the Capitol that re-examine the Temple of Mercury initially signalled by Ballu in Sept années de découvertes (1911), p. 29. Christofle confirms the temple's existence but corrects the orientation: the building is clearly oriented N.-S., NOT E.-W. as Ballu had stated. The cella rested on three small barrel-vaulted rooms; an excellent E.-W. cross-wall is interpreted as part of the temple precinct enclosure. A larger platform of pebble-mortar concrete (cailloutis), 22 × 33 m, lay 10 m from the south wall of the Capitol courtyard on the axis of the cella, oriented N.W.-S.E.; a third monument c. 10 × 22 m, oriented N.-S., was identified some 10 m further away. A post-Roman cemetery — interpreted by Christofle as Berber or possibly Arab on the basis of W.-E. orientation, lack of grave goods in male burials, and bead necklaces of carnelian, painted glass, or coral plus two bronze bracelets in female burials — was installed across this hill. Note: this row's House Name says 'au Nord du Capitole' but its Mapping Notes and Location columns both say 'South of Capitol' — the pre-existing discrepancy is unresolved; the Christofle 1938 evidence pertains specifically to the hill SOUTH of the Capitol. [Source: Christofle 1938 (BIAA-Af-Alg-24): pp. 355-356]

houses.name: Storehouse (Entrepôt)
houses.area_raw: ~1 725 m² (derived from 25 x 69 m, Ballu 1911 III: 53 n. 1; not a published figure)
houses.first_published_by: Ballu, BCTH 1906 (first report); first full treatment Ballu 1911 III: 49-53 [Germain 1969: 88]
houses.key_references: Ballu III: 49-53; Ballu, Rapport fouilles 1905 (BCTH vol. 1906): 201-210, pl. LVIII; Christofle, Rapport 1927-1929 (publ. 1930): 58-62, plan p. 59; Courtois: 82; Germain 1969: 88-90, fig. 12; Gsell AA f. 27, 255, 56; Inv. Mos. III: 95-98; L'Architecture 1913: 99; Christofle 1930: 58-62; Laghmouche 2024: 254, Table 1; Assassi & Mebarki 2021
houses.notes: Christofle 1938 (p. 359, section '3° FOUILLES AU NORD DU DECUMANUS MAXIMUS EN FACE LE CIMETIERE CHRETIEN ET LE LIEU DIT « ENTREPOT »') cites the Entrepôt as a topographical landmark when describing 1933 excavations on the north side of the Decumanus Maximus opposite the Christian cemetery. The 50 × 32 m excavation behind three lowered sidewalk kerbs (cart ruts still visible) revealed three contiguous private Roman houses: (A) an easternmost house with a portico supported by 6 square pilasters 0.50 m on a side (bases and lower piers in place); (B) a middle house with vestibule giving onto a paved courtyard around a 5 m-deep well (its upper part masonry, lower part dry-stone) — fragments of a fine bronze palm recovered from the well shaft; grooves 0.20 m wide in the surrounding paving once held vertical slabs forming the well-curb (margelle); (C) a westernmost house, the most damaged, immediately adjacent to the Lambèse Gate — interior divisions wholly lost. These three houses lie immediately north of/opposite the Entrepôt and would be the closest known elite domestic neighbours to it. [Source: Christofle 1938 (BIAA-Af-Alg-24): p. 359]

houses.name: Great House Over the Pagan Necropolis (Grande maison sur la nécropole païenne ouest de la porte de Lambèse)
houses.name_en: Great House Over the Pagan Necropolis

houses.building_type: House (late phase, constructed entirely with spolia from demolished funerary monuments)
houses.area_raw: ~870 m² (rectangle approximation; interior arrangement partly recoverable)
houses.notes: Christofle 1938 (pp. 359-361, section '4° CONTINUATION DES FOUILLES DE LA NECROPOLE PAIENNE') describes a great house (grande maison) installed after the pagan necropolis on the western side of the second ravine in the direction of Lambèse. Direct translation of the key passage: 'A great house was installed afterwards over this part of the necropolis. Its walls, however, are built with mortar and have a fairly fine appearance, but the builders quite naturally used the materials they had at hand, and all the funerary monuments were demolished. Thus an entablature with decorated soffit, three-banded architrave, and a frieze bearing an inscription was used as a doorjamb, and the upper moulding of the architrave, which would have hindered the door's closure, was hammered down. In another wall, funerary cippi placed upright on edge serve as upright stones (jambs). The east façade of the house is completely cleared; it is 30.45 m long and pierced by a small doorway 1.38 m wide, the only entrance discovered so far. The south façade, also cleared over a length of 28.65 m, offers no passage. Between the east façade and the ravine, I counted 110 tile-tombs, and, unlike what existed in the already-cleared parts of this necropolis, I found skeletons in several of those tombs.' Within the cleared area Christofle records the 'maison de colonnes énormes': two rows of four enormous Corinthian column bases in place, with one wall of the great house separating the rows. He notes this puzzles him ('Ce que je m'explique mal, c'est la présence, dans la partie dégagée, de cette maison de colonnes énormes') and speculates the columns were knocked down the same day by an earthquake. This colossal-column structure is almost certainly an earlier monumental building (temple, basilica, or large peristyle of a vanished elite domus) over which the great house was later built. Not given its own row in this database because its identification as a 'house' is uncertain — it is recorded here as a feature of this row.

houses.notes: Christofle 1938 (pp. 356-357) describes a fragment of an earlier Roman house uncovered while excavating the Christian cemetery at the Lambèse Gate. Direct translation (from section '2° FOUILLES DU CIMETIERE CHRETIEN DE LA PORTE DE LAMBESE'): 'In carrying out these excavations, I recovered a sandstone paving with the emplacement of a basin from the courtyard of a house, and also an apsed room heated from below (the remains, no doubt, of a small private bath). The hypocaust pilae are all in place, and the mouth of the furnace is well preserved. Four sandstone columns, lying on their sides in this room, have been re-erected on their bases, found in place.' Key features: paved courtyard with basin emplacement; apsed room with intact hypocaust pilae and well-preserved furnace mouth (interpreted by Christofle as a small private bath); four sandstone columns originally upright in the apsed room, re-erected on their in-situ bases. The 1908 mosaic-lift work in this cemetery (Ballu) had not gone below tomb-floor level, so the domus underneath had not previously been recognized. This row is necessarily fragmentary and its full plan will remain unrecoverable while the Christian cemetery overlay is left in place.; The 1908 work at this cemetery had only lifted the mosaics covering the tombs without excavating below, which is why the underlying domus had not previously been recognised; 73 tombs cleared this campaign [christofle_1938 printed p. 358]

houses.notes: BCB 1905: atrium ~10 m square with a ~2 m-wide portico of ten columns (four wide, three deep); central well ~9 m deep in the atrium; entrance vestibule ~5 m wide; tablinum floor a geometric mosaic with vegetal ornament; geometric mosaics (brown/yellow) under the atrium porticoes [BCB 1905: 90].; 21 m x 24 m footprint; entrance 2.10 m; atrium 10.50 x 10.60 m [ballu_1897b_ruines_I printed p. 224]; Portico on the Decumanus carried by eight square pillars (only footings remain) [ballu_1897b_ruines_I printed p. 224]; Planter opening of 2.20 m opposite the entrance; bifrons tragic-mask heads crowned the stone uprights (fig. 37) [ballu_1897b_ruines_I printed p. 224]; Tablinum reached through three bays on two columns; fauces each side leading to corner alae; these bound the house on the south [ballu_1897b_ruines_I printed p. 226]; Ballu: house stood in a zone reserved for public buildings; probably the residence of a magistrate or important personage [ballu_1897b_ruines_I printed p. 226]; BCB 1905 pp. 88-92 with plan fig. 40; Inv. Mos. III 146-147 [germain_1969_a printed p. 37]; Ballu 1903 notes the house's columns were re-erected; view given as Fig. 21 [ballu_1903_II printed p. 110]; Ballu 1909 rapport: the street west of a NE-quarter insula is 'la voie dite de la maison aux jardinieres', the only paved one around that block [Ballu 1909 - Rapport fouilles BIAA.pdf printed p. houses.name: Ballu 1903 House 1 (La première)
houses.notes: Source: 20.90 (N-S) x 22.80 (E-W) [ballu_1903_II printed p. 95]; Portico on the Cardo carried by two square piers and five columns; six steps kept it level against the street slope [ballu_1903_II printed p. 95]; Equidistant from the petits Thermes Nord and the Schola, separated from each by two Decumanus widths and one (uncleared) insula [ballu_1903_II printed p. 95]; E-W wall splits house in two: south part with atrium (stone enclosures, three columns preserved), antechamber east, two unequal rooms; north part central room + six rooms radiating; atrium keeps part of its paving [ballu_1903_II printed p. 95]

houses.name: Ballu 1903 House 8 (La huitième)
houses.notes: Isolated residential building with dimensions 29 x 24.20 m.; Portico of nine bays on Cardo Maximus side, seven bays on Decumanus Maximus side [ballu_1903_II printed p. 98]; Two large shops (boutiques) on the Decumanus, each divided in two; corner shop had a cellar [ballu_1903_II printed p. 98]; Entrance with two-column porch on Forum street leading to a paved vestibule and paved atrium; hemispherical fountain on south side of atrium [ballu_1903_II printed p. 99]

houses.name: Ballu 1903 House 9 (La neuvième)
houses.notes: Isolated residential building with dimensions 29 x 20 m.; Ground-floor plan: 6-bay portico on the grande voie sheltering 4 shops (three widely open) [ballu_1903_II printed p. 98]

houses.name: Ballu 1903 House 10 (La dixième)
houses.notes: 28.95 x 20.80 [ballu_1903_II printed p. 99]; Remains of a staircase with return landing 'which served to go up to the first floor' - explicit upper storey [ballu_1903_II printed p. 99]; Entrance from the voie de la Basilique Byzantine into a large paved vestibule followed by a smaller one; eleven further rooms; in-place stone rainwater downpipe on the outside of the north wall [ballu_1903_II printed p. 99]; Seven portico bays on the Decumanus Maximus [ballu_1903_II printed p. 99]

houses.name: Ballu 1903 House 11 (La onzième)
houses.notes: Isolated residential building with dimensions 28.90 x 20.90 m.; Divided into two nearly equal halves by a N-S wall [ballu_1903_II printed p. 100]; Two boutiques open on the portico + small magasin in SE corner (east half) [ballu_1903_II printed p. 100]; East half: 9 salles + encroachment room on 3rd Cardo; west half: 3 rooms under portico (one w/ 3-step stair), 2 stone-paved rooms, 2 w/ paving traces, 3 other chambers [ballu_1903_II printed p. 100]; Staircase of three steps in a room under the portico (west half) [ballu_1903_II printed p. 100]

houses.name: Ballu 1903 House 12 (La douzième)
houses.notes: Isolated residential building with dimensions 25 x variable m.; Four shops with wide openings on the triumphal-way portico; eleven rooms up to a wall parallel to it [ballu_1903_II printed p. 100]; Beyond the wall parallel to the Decumanus Maximus, fourteen further cleared rooms, plus three small rooms won from the 4th cardo [ballu_1903_II printed p. 101]; A covered passage 5 m wide was built over the street (voie de Trajan side) [ballu_1903_II printed p. 100]

houses.name: Ballu 1903 House 4 (La quatrième)
houses.notes: Isolated residential building with dimensions 20.25 x 21.40 m.; Portico of 5 columns + 2 square piers on the Cardo Maximus front [ballu_1903_II printed p. 96]; Divided into two equal portions by an E-W wall; S part atrium + 6 rooms (one w/ mosaic fragment); N part 6 rooms, linked by three wide doors [ballu_1903_II printed p. 96]; Diana/Actaeon panel: signature inscription SELIVS P G, restored Seliu[s] p(in)g(ebat); jewelled figures; removed to Museum for its colours [germain_1969_a printed p. 21]; NW-corner room (6.60 x 5) with figured mosaic; S-part room with mosaic paving fragment [germain_1969_a printed p. 19]

houses.name: Ballu 1903 House 5 (La cinquième)
houses.notes: Isolated residential building with dimensions 21.10 x 21 m.; West strip 6 m wide with four rooms apparently used as shops [ballu_1903_II printed p. 97]; Atrium retaining several columns and a rectangular basin [ballu_1903_II printed p. 97]

houses.name: Ballu 1903 House 6 (La sixième)
houses.notes: Isolated residential building with dimensions 21.20 x 21.25 m.; West part divided by a N-S wall into two large divisions with a room 10 x 10.80 m and another 9.90 x 10 m; east part has nine rooms, one apsidal (hemispherical). A cistern and atrium with columns/basin were noted for the adjacent (fifth) house. [ballu_1903_II printed p. 98]

houses.name: Ballu 1903 House 20 (La vingtième)

houses.key_references: Christofle 1938 (Rapport 1933-1936): 359 [corrected: Section is on printed p. 359 (pdf 364), NOT 358 — christofle_1938 printed p. 359, audit 2026-07-05]
houses.notes: Christofle 1938 (p. 358) description (direct translation): 'The second house is in no better state. Once the vestibule was passed, one arrived in a fairly vast courtyard, paved in the area surrounding a well in good condition. This well was completely excavated and was 5 metres deep. The fragments of a fine bronze palm were recovered in it. It was masonry-built in its upper part and, for the rest, built of dry stone. The water table was not reached. In the paving that surrounds it, one can see grooves 0.20 m wide and a few centimetres deep, grooves that received vertical slabs forming the well-curb (margelle). Nothing remains of the apartments that gave onto this courtyard.' Key features preserved: vestibule, paved courtyard, 5 m masonry-then-dry-stone well, slab-curb sockets in the paving, fragments of a fine bronze palm recovered from the well shaft.

houses.name: Ballu 1903 House 2 (La deuxième)
houses.notes: Isolated residential house.; Owner Lucius Julius Januarius, established by two inscriptions: statues of Aesculapius and of Hygie given by his son-in-law Lucius Acilius Granianus 'ad exornationem balinei' [ballu_1903_II printed p. 32]; Seven rooms in the ~20 x 20 m insula square, plus a very complete balineum in the NW part (mosaic vestibule, cold pool with wall-painting traces and three steps, caldarium with semicircular west end, twin-walled hemispherical alveus, thick-walled étuve, stoking room) [ballu_1903_II printed p. 31]; On the east the owner annexed the public way: a 6.60 m room, well-preserved latrines with drain channel, and a portico on one square pier + two columns; the advance onto the street was 2.60 m [ballu_1903_II printed p. 31]; SW fraction destroyed by the Byzantine basilica (built partly of the house's materials); three Christian tombs found on the atrium paving; entrance vestibule paved, open to the street on the north [ballu_1903_II printed p. 30]; Gsell AA f. 27, 255, 9; de Pachtère Inv. Mos. III, 129-130; Courtois, Timgad, p. 48; plan: Ballu 1903 pl. VII ('Basilique chrétienne, baptistère et maison de Januarius. Plan', facing p. 34) [germain_1969_a printed p. 16]
